Neonates of Eurytemora affinis emerge from the brood sac at a total length at birth of 0.013 cm [Lb = 0.013 cm], a diminutive size typical of calanoid copepods. This initial stage is followed by a period of rapid somatic growth through six naupliar instars before the transition to the first copepodite stage. At metamorphosis from the last nauplius to the first copepodite, individuals measure approximately 0.05 cm  in total length, a milestone that marks the beginning of the accelerating juvenile phase. The corresponding dry weight at this developmental inflection point is remarkably low, with field-collected specimens yielding a mean value of 0.1526 micrograms , calculated from established length-weight regressions; this value is a key determinant of lipid reserves necessary for the energy-intensive transition to the predatory copepodite stage. This combined larval-juvenile phase is characterized by intense feeding on phytoplankton and suspended particulates, with individuals progressing through five copepodite instars. The rapid mass gain during this interval is essential for accumulating the energetic reserves necessary to meet the elevated basal maintenance requirements of the maturing copepodite.

Reproductive maturity in this species is attained at a total length at puberty of 0.149 cm [Lp = 0.149 cm], which corresponds to an ultimate total length of 0.149 cm [Li = 0.149 cm] for the adult female. The dry weight at puberty has been documented at 5.081 micrograms , a value that also represents the ultimate dry weight of 5.081 micrograms  in gravid individuals. These adult measurements indicate that somatic growth effectively ceases upon the onset of reproductive activity, a pattern commonly observed in semelparous or iteroparous copepods with indeterminate growth potential. The attainment of this terminal size is concomitant with the formation of the first ovigerous female, which carries a single egg sac attached to the genital segment. In laboratory cultures fed a mixed diet of Rhodomonas and Thalassiosira, ovigerous females produce approximately 110 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 110 eggs per clutch], with a clutch frequency of one clutch every three days [F_R_i = one clutch every three days]. This reproductive output was measured under controlled thermal conditions of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], reflecting the maximum daily egg production that the species can sustain under optimal food availability. The synchrony between puberty and the cessation of external growth suggests a strong trade-off between somatic investment and immediate reproductive effort.

Puberty itself is reached during the fifth copepodite stage, when the developing gonads first become histologically distinguishable from somatic tissue. In contrast to the first reproduction event, which occurs shortly after the final molt to adulthood, the physiological process of sexual maturation begins earlier, with the onset of gametogenesis marking the initiation of the reproductively viable organism. At this point, the total length at birth of 0.013 cm [Lb = 0.013 cm] has increased more than tenfold, illustrating the extreme allometric growth that characterizes the accelerating juvenile phase. The corresponding dry weight at birth is merely 0.012 micrograms , highlighting the substantial increase in biomass that must occur before the first ovigerous female can be produced. This nearly 400-fold increase in dry mass from birth to puberty underscores the strong selective pressure on growth efficiency and food acquisition during the pre-reproductive interval. In nature, this phase is constrained by seasonal phytoplankton blooms, with delayed maturation observed under low-food conditions in both field and laboratory settings. The ability to buffer developmental delays through lipid storage is a key adaptation for surviving periods of resource scarcity in temperate and subarctic estuaries.

The maximum lifespan of Eurytemora affinis under laboratory conditions is 72 days [am = 72 days], a longevity that is strongly dependent on ambient temperature at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This value was recorded in animals maintained at a constant temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], which slows metabolic rates and extends the duration of both the pre-reproductive and reproductive phases. At this lower temperature, the interval between sequential clutches is prolonged, with the one clutch every three days [F_R_i = one clutch every three days] schedule observed at 22 °C being replaced by a significantly reduced frequency. The dry weight at metamorphosis of 0.1526 micrograms  serves as a critical benchmark for determining whether an individual will successfully navigate the transition to adulthood under such thermally constrained conditions. Field studies in the St. Lawrence estuary indicate that spring-spawning cohorts experiencing rapid warming exhibit compressed generation times, while autumn cohorts at lower temperatures display extended development. Post-reproductive mortality typically follows the final clutch deposition, with females showing progressive deterioration of the digestive tract and loss of body condition over the subsequent week. The ultimate dry weight of 5.081 micrograms  declines rapidly after the cessation of feeding, as the animal catabolizes its remaining tissues to meet maintenance costs.

Comparative life-history analyses across the genus Eurytemora reveal that E. affinis occupies an intermediate position along the fast-slow continuum, with its ultimate total length of 0.149 cm [Li = 0.149 cm] placing it among the smaller-bodied members of the clade. Congeneric species such as Eurytemora herdmani achieve larger asymptotic sizes and correspondingly greater clutch volumes, while Eurytemora americana exhibits a more compressed generation time. The total length at birth of 0.013 cm [Lb = 0.013 cm] is broadly conserved across the genus, suggesting strong phylogenetic constraints on egg size and naupliar morphology. The maximum reproductive rate observed under optimal conditions reflects the production of approximately 110 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 110 eggs per clutch] with a clutch frequency of one clutch every three days [F_R_i = one clutch every three days] at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], yielding a substantial per capita contribution to population growth. At the cooler temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the maximum lifespan of 72 days [am = 72 days] allows for the production of several successive clutches, though total lifetime fecundity is reduced relative to warm-acclimated individuals. The dry weight of 5.081 micrograms  at puberty is consistent with the energetic requirements of egg production in small calanoids, where maternal investment per clutch represents a significant fraction of somatic mass. These demographic parameters position E. affinis as a highly adaptable estuarine colonizer capable of rapid numerical response to favorable conditions, while its physiological tolerance allows persistence across a wide thermal gradient.
